newsitem.title: CANADA: Greyhound sets deadline on air success.
newsitem.headline: Greyhound sets deadline on air success.

text.p: Greyhound Canada Transportation Corp, battered by the rocky startup of its no-frills air travel service, is giving the operation until the end of this summer to become successful, the company's chief executive said.
If by then Greyhound Air does not straighten up and fly right, the company will bid farewell to Canada's airline industry, Greyhound's Dick Huisman said.
"We believe that if we go through the summer we will be able to prove this is a viable business," Huisman told reporters after the company's annual meeting.
"If we can't we will make the right decision to exit."

The company, with much fanfare, announced last spring it would launch Greyhound Air, following a corporate restructuring, which resulted in charter bus services being spun off, and a deal with Kelowna Flightcraft Air Charter Ltd, which supplied the aircraft and flight services.

However, Canada's National Transportation Agency denied Greyhound approvals to operate the service. It wasn't until the federal Cabinet overturned the NTA decision after a costly delay that it took off in July, throwing a spanner into the firm's revenue projections.

Greyhound, which posted losses in its first abbreviated fiscal year after restructuring and in the first quarter of 1997, lost about C$14 million in potential revenues because of the delays, Huisman said.
The company's shares, which climbed to 7.00 after the restructuring, have been hammered by investors since the launch of Greyhound Air. They were trading at 3.00 on Friday.

Huisman said the company had retained Boston-based airline consultancy SH&E in efforts to boost revenues and returns from Greyhound Air over the next few months, but declined to disclose proposed new strategies for competitive reasons.
However, the company's decision to start selling tickets through travel agencies, as opposed to only its own reservation network, was supported by the consultants, he said.
A cutback in weekend flight frequency in April and May and a decision to add one more Edmonton-Winnipeg-Toronto flight per day this summer.
Huisman said he remained optimistic that Greyhound's plans for a low-cost air service that meshed its core bus network would prove successful and Greyhound would be profitable in 1997.

But the strength of its bus and courier services could allow the firm to drop Greyhound Air if needed, he said, citing analyst estimates that place the value of the company without air at C$5.20 per share.
"We are not betting the farm. If the decision would be made to exit, which I'm not contemplating by a long shot, we believe in the value of the core business," he said.
He said competition with Canada's two major air carriers and rival western Canadian discount flyer WestJet Ltd, was not a major factor in Greyhound Air's poor returns so far.
He said WestJet, which flies in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, had more impact on its bus ridership because of similar fare prices.
